title: A blocking queue
description:
The workhorse of multi-threaded programs: one or more **producer** threads put items in, one or more **consumer** threads take them out, and a consumer that finds the queue empty **sleeps** until something arrives instead of spinning.

Write `template <typename T> class BlockingQueue`:

- `void push(T value)`: adds an item and wakes one waiting consumer.
- `std::optional<T> pop()`: removes and returns the oldest item. If the queue is empty it waits. It returns `std::nullopt` only when the queue is empty **and** has been closed.
- `void close()`: no more items will come; wakes every waiting consumer so they can finish.

You need a `std::mutex`, a `std::condition_variable`, a `std::queue<T>` and a `bool` for "closed".

Waiting looks like this. The lambda is the condition to wait **for**; it protects against waking up for no reason and against notifications that arrived before the wait began.

```cpp
std::unique_lock lock{ m_mutex };
m_ready.wait(lock, [this] { return !m_items.empty() || m_closed; });
```
hints: Keep a `std::deque<T>`, a `std::mutex`, a `std::condition_variable` and a `bool closed`.

`pop` waits with `m_cv.wait(lock, [this] { return !m_items.empty() || m_closed; });`; after waking, an empty queue means it was closed: return `std::nullopt`. `push` and `close` notify (`notify_one`, `notify_all`).
lessonTitle: Condition Variables, Semaphores, Latches and Barriers
